etymology: From the Greek speirō, “to sow,” the husbandman who casts seed; the parable of the four soils in which the seed is the Word of God.
biblical_def: The parable of the Sower stands first among the parables of the kingdom, and the LORD Himself called it the key to the rest: Know ye not this parable? and how then will ye know all parables? (Mar 4:13). A sower went forth to sow, and the seed fell upon four kinds of ground (Mat 13:3). Some fell by the way side, and the fowls came and devoured it up; some upon stony places, where it sprang up quickly but withered for want of root; some among thorns, which sprang up and choked it; and other fell into good ground, and brought forth fruit, some an hundredfold, some sixtyfold, some thirtyfold (Mat 13:4-8). The seed is the word of the kingdom (Mat 13:19), and the soils are the hearts of men that hear it. He that received seed into the good ground is he that heareth the word, and understandeth it; which also beareth fruit (Mat 13:23). The dictionary marks this parable as the great teaching on the Word and the heart. The same seed is cast on every ground, yet only the good ground bears fruit; and the good ground is not made good by itself, for by nature the heart is stony and thorny and trodden hard. So the Scripture teaches that fruit springs only where sovereign and effectual grace has prepared the soil, breaking up the fallow ground and giving the increase. The Word is the appointed means; the new heart is the gift of God; and the fruit, in patience, is the certain mark of the regenerate (Luk 8:15).
webster_summary: The parable in which a sower casts seed on four soils, picturing the Word received in hearts prepared by sovereign grace.
webster_full: THE SOWER, the parable of the four soils, first and chief of the kingdom parables.
The sower casts seed, which is the word of the kingdom, upon every kind of ground.
Three soils — the way side, the stony, the thorny — bear no abiding fruit.
The good ground heareth, understandeth, and bringeth forth fruit thirty, sixty, and an hundredfold.
The good ground is the heart prepared by effectual grace to receive the Word.
scriptures: Mat 13:3

Mar 4:13
And he said unto them, Know ye not this parable? and how then will ye know all parables?

Luk 8:15
But that on the good ground are they, which in an honest and good heart, having heard the word, keep it, and bring forth fruit with patience.
corruption_summary: A parable of the kingdom plainly teaching that fruit springs only where grace prepares the heart; it has drawn little redefinition.
corruption_paragraphs: The parable of the Sower has drawn little redefinition from the present age, surviving as a familiar and beloved teaching of the LORD. The dictionary records it that the reader may mark the Word as the appointed seed and the prepared heart as the good ground in which alone it bears fruit.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the same Word falls on every heart, yet bears fruit only in the good ground, and the good ground is the heart that sovereign grace has prepared. The way side, the stony, and the thorny are not made fruitful by better sowing or by their own resolve; the increase is God’s. So the Scripture humbles the hearer and casts him upon the grace that gives both the seed and the soil; and it bids him take heed how he hear, for the abiding fruit, brought forth with patience, is the certain mark of a heart renewed by the LORD.

etymology: From the Greek zizanion, the darnel weed that mimics wheat until the ear appears; the parable of the field sown with good seed and tares.
biblical_def: The parable of the Wheat and the Tares teaches the mingling of the good and the evil in the world until the harvest at the end of the age. The kingdom of heaven is likened unto a man which sowed good seed in his field; but while men slept, his enemy came and sowed tares among the wheat, and went his way (Mat 13:24-25). When the blade sprang up, the tares appeared also; and the servants would have gathered them at once, but the householder forbade them, Let both grow together until the harvest, lest while ye gather up the tares, ye root up also the wheat with them (Mat 13:30). The LORD Himself expounded it: He that soweth the good seed is the Son of man; the field is the world; the good seed are the children of the kingdom; but the tares are the children of the wicked one; the enemy that sowed them is the devil; the harvest is the end of the world; and the reapers are the angels (Mat 13:37-39). The dictionary marks this parable as the great word on patience and judgment. The field is the world, not the church only, and in it the righteous and the wicked grow side by side, not to be severed by the hand of man. So the Scripture teaches that the separation belongs to God, and is reserved to the last day, when the Son of man shall send forth His angels, and they shall gather out of His kingdom all things that offend, and cast them into a furnace of fire; then shall the righteous shine forth as the sun (Mat 13:41-43).
webster_summary: The parable in which wheat and tares grow together in the field of the world until the angels sever them at the harvest of judgment.
webster_full: THE WHEAT AND THE TARES, the parable of the field sown with good seed and with tares.
The good seed is the children of the kingdom; the tares are the children of the wicked one.
The field is the world, where the righteous and the wicked grow together.
The householder forbids the servants to root up the tares before the harvest.
At the end of the world the angels sever the wicked from the just for judgment.
scriptures: Let both grow together until the harvest: and in the time of harvest I will say to the reapers, Gather ye together first the tares, and bind them in bundles to burn them: but gather the wheat into my barn.
The field is the world; the good seed are the children of the kingdom; but the tares are the children of the wicked one;
The enemy that sowed them is the devil; the harvest is the end of the world; and the reapers are the angels.

corruption_summary: A parable of the kingdom teaching the patient mingling of good and evil until the final judgment; it has drawn little redefinition.
corruption_paragraphs: The parable of the Wheat and the Tares has drawn little redefinition from the present age, surviving as the LORD’s own teaching on the field of the world and the harvest at the end. The dictionary records it that the reader may mark the patience of God in the present mingling and the certainty of the severing to come.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the separation of the righteous and the wicked belongs to God and is reserved to the last day. The field is the world, where wheat and tares grow together; the servants are not to root up the tares before the harvest, for that judgment is the angels’ work at the end of the age. So the Scripture forbids both a careless tolerance that denies any harvest and a hasty zeal that would sever now what God reserves to Himself; and it sets before the children of the kingdom the day when they shall shine forth as the sun, and the wicked be cast into the furnace of fire.

etymology: From the Greek sinapi, the mustard plant, whose seed is least of all seeds; the parable of the kingdom’s small beginning and great growth.
biblical_def: The parable of the Mustard Seed teaches the small beginning and the great increase of the kingdom of heaven. The kingdom of heaven, said the LORD, is like to a grain of mustard seed, which a man took, and sowed in his field: which indeed is the least of all seeds; but when it is grown, it is the greatest among herbs, and becometh a tree, so that the birds of the air come and lodge in the branches thereof (Mat 13:31-32). The dictionary marks this parable as the great word of comfort against the smallness of beginnings. The kingdom in its first appearing was a despised and lowly thing — a Babe in a manger, a company of unlettered fishermen, a Master crucified between thieves; the least of all seeds in the eyes of men. Yet from that seed has grown the greatest of trees, and the nations of the earth have come to lodge in its branches. So the Scripture teaches that the increase is of God, who chooses the foolish things of the world to confound the wise, and the weak things to confound the things which are mighty (1Co 1:27). The mustard seed has in it a life and an appointed growth that no man gives and no man can stay; and the kingdom of Christ, sown small and weak, grows by the secret power of God until it fills the earth. Let no believer despise the day of small things (Zec 4:10), for the seed of the kingdom carries within it the certainty of its own great increase.
webster_summary: The parable in which the kingdom, least of all seeds, grows into the greatest of herbs where the birds lodge.
webster_full: THE MUSTARD SEED, the parable of the kingdom’s small beginning and great growth.
The grain of mustard seed is the least of all seeds when it is sown.
When grown, it becometh the greatest among herbs and a tree.
The birds of the air come and lodge in the branches thereof.
The kingdom, sown small and weak, grows by the secret power of God.

corruption_summary: A parable of the kingdom teaching its small beginning and great increase by the power of God; it has drawn little redefinition.
corruption_paragraphs: The parable of the Mustard Seed has drawn little redefinition from the present age, surviving as a plain and cheering word of the kingdom’s growth. The dictionary records it that the reader may mark the smallness of the seed and the greatness of the tree, and may not despise the day of small things.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the increase of the kingdom is of God, who makes the least of seeds become the greatest of herbs. The kingdom of Christ began small and despised in the eyes of men, yet has grown until the nations lodge in its branches; for the seed carries within it a life and an appointed growth that no man gives and none can stay. So the Scripture comforts the saint against the smallness of present things, and teaches that God chooses the weak to confound the mighty, and brings His kingdom to its great increase by His own secret and certain power.
roots_summary: From the Greek sinapi, the mustard plant, the parable names the kingdom’s least seed and greatest tree.

etymology: From the Greek zumē, leaven or yeast; the parable of the kingdom hid in three measures of meal until the whole is leavened.
biblical_def: The parable of the Leaven is the companion of the Mustard Seed, teaching the pervasive and hidden working of the kingdom of heaven. The kingdom of heaven, said the LORD, is like unto leaven, which a woman took, and hid in three measures of meal, till the whole was leavened (Mat 13:33). The dictionary marks this parable as the great word on the inward and secret power of the kingdom. Where the Mustard Seed shows the kingdom’s outward growth from small to great, the Leaven shows its inward and silent spread, working unseen until the whole lump is changed. The leaven is hid in the meal, and no eye marks its working; yet it ceases not until all is leavened through and through. So the Scripture teaches that the kingdom of God comes not with observation (Luk 17:20), but works secretly and irresistibly, transforming the heart it enters and spreading through the whole mass of a man, a household, a people, until all is changed by its power. Though leaven is elsewhere in Scripture a figure of corruption that must be purged, here the LORD takes it for the hidden and unstoppable might of His grace, which, once hid in the soul, leavens the whole, and once hid in the world, fails not till the meal of the nations is leavened. The kingdom works not by the noise of men but by the quiet, sovereign, and certain operation of God.
webster_summary: The parable in which the kingdom, like leaven hid in meal, works secretly and irresistibly until the whole is leavened.
webster_full: THE LEAVEN, the parable of the kingdom hid in three measures of meal.
A woman took leaven and hid it in the meal until the whole was leavened.
The leaven works unseen, picturing the kingdom’s hidden and inward spread.
The kingdom of God cometh not with observation, but works secretly and irresistibly.
Once hid in the soul or the world, the leaven fails not till all is changed.

corruption_paragraphs: The parable of the Leaven has drawn little redefinition from the present age, surviving as the companion of the Mustard Seed in the LORD’s teaching on the kingdom’s growth. The dictionary records it that the reader may mark the inward and secret power by which the kingdom spreads till the whole is leavened.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the kingdom of God works inwardly, secretly, and irresistibly, like leaven hid in meal. It comes not with observation, nor by the noise and force of men, but by the quiet and sovereign operation of God, which, once hid in a soul, transforms the whole man, and, once hid in the world, ceases not till the meal of the nations is leavened through. So the Scripture teaches the saint not to measure the kingdom’s progress by what the eye can see, but to trust the certain and unstoppable power of the grace that God has hid in the lump.
roots_summary: From the Greek zumē, leaven, the parable names the kingdom’s hidden and pervasive working in the meal.

etymology: From the Greek thēsauros, treasure; the parable of the treasure hid in a field, for which a man sold all that he had.
biblical_def: The parable of the Hidden Treasure teaches the surpassing worth of the kingdom of heaven and the gladness with which it is bought. Again, the kingdom of heaven, said the LORD, is like unto treasure hid in a field; the which when a man hath found, he hideth, and for joy thereof goeth and selleth all that he hath, and buyeth that field (Mat 13:44). The dictionary marks this parable as the great word on the worth of the kingdom and the affection of the heart that finds it. The man stumbles upon the treasure, not by long searching but as one to whom it is shown; and having found it, he counts all else as nothing, and for joy thereof sells all that he has to make it his own. So the Scripture teaches that the kingdom of God, and Christ who is its King and its riches, are of a worth that exceeds all the world, and that the soul which has been given eyes to see it will gladly part with all to gain it. This is no purchase of merit, as if a man could buy heaven with his goods; the selling of all is the parting with every rival treasure, the counting of all things but loss for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus the Lord (Phi 3:8). And the joy is the mark of the work of grace: the heart that has found the treasure does not grudge the price, but for joy thereof gives up all, esteeming the field with its hidden riches far above whatsoever it forsakes.
webster_summary: The parable in which a man, finding treasure hid in a field, for joy sells all that he has to buy it.
webster_full: THE HIDDEN TREASURE, the parable of the treasure found in a field.
A man finds the treasure hid in a field and hides it again.
For joy thereof he goeth and selleth all that he hath.
He buyeth that field to make the treasure his own.
The treasure pictures the surpassing worth of the kingdom and of Christ its King.

corruption_summary: A parable of the kingdom teaching its surpassing worth and the joy of forsaking all to gain it; it has drawn little redefinition.
corruption_paragraphs: The parable of the Hidden Treasure has drawn little redefinition from the present age, surviving as a plain word on the worth of the kingdom and the joy of him who finds it. The dictionary records it that the reader may mark the gladness with which the treasure is bought and the all that is forsaken to gain it.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the kingdom of heaven, and Christ who is its riches, are of a worth surpassing all the world, so that the soul given eyes to see it gladly parts with everything to gain it. The selling of all is no purchase of merit, but the counting of all things but loss for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ; and the joy is the very mark of grace, for the heart that has found the treasure does not grudge the price. So the Scripture searches the affections, and asks where the treasure of a man truly lies, knowing that there will his heart be also.

etymology: From the Greek margaritēs, pearl; the parable of the merchant who sold all to buy one pearl of great price.
biblical_def: The parable of the Pearl of Great Price is the companion of the Hidden Treasure, teaching the same surpassing worth of the kingdom under another figure. Again, the kingdom of heaven, said the LORD, is like unto a merchant man, seeking goodly pearls: who, when he had found one pearl of great price, went and sold all that he had, and bought it (Mat 13:45-46). The dictionary marks this parable beside its fellow, yet with a difference the reader should mark. The man in the field stumbles upon his treasure unsought; the merchant is one that seeks goodly pearls, and finds among them the one pearl that surpasses all. So the Scripture sets forth two ways in which the kingdom is found: it comes upon some as a free and sudden discovery, and is given to others as the end of a long seeking that the LORD Himself has set in the heart. Yet in both the price is one — he sold all that he had, and bought it. The pearl is Christ and His kingdom, of a worth above all the goodly things a man has gathered; and the merchant, having found it, parts with every lesser pearl to make it his own. The selling of all is not the wage that purchases the pearl, for grace is free; it is the gladness of a heart that has seen the one thing worth all, and will keep back nothing to possess it. There is but one pearl of great price, and Christ is He.
webster_summary: The parable in which a merchant, finding one pearl of great price, sells all his goodly pearls to buy it.
webster_full: THE PEARL OF GREAT PRICE, the parable of the merchant and the one surpassing pearl.
The merchant man seeketh goodly pearls.
He findeth one pearl of great price above all the rest.
He went and sold all that he had, and bought it.
The pearl pictures Christ and His kingdom, of a worth above all things.

corruption_paragraphs: The parable of the Pearl of Great Price has drawn little redefinition from the present age, surviving as the companion of the Hidden Treasure in the LORD’s teaching on the worth of the kingdom. The dictionary records it that the reader may mark the one pearl that surpasses all, for which the merchant gladly sells every lesser thing.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that there is one pearl of great price, and Christ is He, of a worth above all the goodly things a man has gathered. The merchant’s selling of all is no wage that buys the pearl, for the grace of God is free; it is the gladness of a heart that has seen the one thing worth all the rest, and will keep back nothing to possess it. So the Scripture teaches the soul to count all things but loss for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ, and to forsake every lesser pearl for the one that is precious above all.
roots_summary: From the Greek margaritēs, pearl, the parable names the one pearl of great price bought with all a man has.

etymology: From the Greek sagēnē, a large seine or dragnet; the parable of the net cast into the sea that gathered of every kind.
biblical_def: The parable of the Dragnet closes the LORD’s teaching of the kingdom parables by the sea, and like the Wheat and Tares it sets before us the judgment at the end of the age. Again, the kingdom of heaven, said the LORD, is like unto a net, that was cast into the sea, and gathered of every kind: which, when it was full, they drew to shore, and sat down, and gathered the good into vessels, but cast the bad away (Mat 13:47-48). Then He gave the meaning: So shall it be at the end of the world: the angels shall come forth, and sever the wicked from among the just, and shall cast them into the furnace of fire: there shall be wailing and gnashing of teeth (Mat 13:49-50). The dictionary marks this parable as a solemn word on the final severing. The net is cast wide and gathers of every kind, good and bad together, even as the visible profession of the kingdom holds within it the true and the false. But the drawing to shore is the end of the world, and then comes the sorting that cannot be undone. So the Scripture teaches that the mingling of the present age is not perpetual, but ends in a fixed and final separation by the hand of God’s angels, in which the wicked are severed from the just and cast into the furnace of fire. This is the eternal conscious judgment the LORD Himself declares, the wailing and gnashing of teeth; and it stands as a warning against every false hope that the bad shall not at last be cast away.
webster_summary: The parable in which a net gathers fish of every kind, and at the end the angels sever the wicked from the just.
webster_full: THE DRAGNET, the parable of the net cast into the sea.
The net is cast wide and gathereth of every kind, good and bad.
When it is full, the good are gathered into vessels and the bad cast away.
So at the end of the world the angels sever the wicked from the just.
The wicked are cast into the furnace of fire, with wailing and gnashing of teeth.

corruption_summary: A parable of the kingdom teaching the final severing of the wicked from the just at the end of the age; it has drawn little redefinition.
corruption_paragraphs: The parable of the Dragnet has drawn little redefinition from the present age, surviving as the LORD’s plain word on the judgment that ends the world. The dictionary records it that the reader may mark the wide net that gathers every kind and the certain severing that comes when it is drawn to shore.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the mingling of the present age is not perpetual, but ends in a fixed and final separation by the hand of God. The net gathers good and bad together, as the visible profession of the kingdom holds the true and the false; but at the end of the world the angels sever the wicked from the just and cast them into the furnace of fire. So the Scripture warns against every soft hope that the bad shall not at last be cast away, and sets the eternal conscious judgment of God — the wailing and gnashing of teeth — before every careless soul that it may flee to Christ while the net is yet in the sea.
roots_summary: From the Greek sagēnē, a dragnet, the parable names the net that gathers every kind till the final severing.

etymology: From the Greek probaton, sheep; the parable of the shepherd who leaves the ninety and nine to seek the one that is lost.
biblical_def: The parable of the Lost Sheep teaches the seeking love of God toward the perishing, and the joy of heaven over the recovery of one sinner. When the Pharisees and scribes murmured that the LORD received sinners and ate with them, He answered with this parable: What man of you, having an hundred sheep, if he lose one of them, doth not leave the ninety and nine in the wilderness, and go after that which is lost, until he find it? And when he hath found it, he layeth it on his shoulders, rejoicing (Luk 15:4-5). And He drew the meaning: I say unto you, that likewise joy shall be in heaven over one sinner that repenteth, more than over ninety and nine just persons, which need no repentance (Luk 15:7). The dictionary marks this parable as the great word on seeking grace. The sheep does not find the shepherd; the shepherd seeks the sheep, and seeks it until he find it, and bears it home upon his own shoulders. So the Scripture teaches that salvation begins not in the sinner’s search for God but in God’s search for the sinner; the Son of man is come to seek and to save that which was lost (Luk 19:10). This is no general benevolence that leaves the finding to the lost one’s own strength, but the effectual seeking of the Good Shepherd, who giveth His life for the sheep and loseth none that the Father hath given Him. And when the lost is found, the joy is heaven’s own; the angels of God rejoice over one sinner that repenteth.
webster_summary: The parable in which a shepherd leaves the ninety and nine to seek one lost sheep, and heaven rejoices over its recovery.

He leaveth the ninety and nine and goeth after the lost sheep until he find it.
He layeth it on his shoulders, rejoicing, and beareth it home.
Joy is in heaven over one sinner that repenteth.
The Son of man is come to seek and to save that which was lost.

Luk 15:7

corruption_summary: A parable of the kingdom teaching the seeking grace of the Good Shepherd and heaven’s joy over the penitent; it has drawn little redefinition.
corruption_paragraphs: The parable of the Lost Sheep has drawn little redefinition from the present age, surviving as a tender and beloved word on the seeking love of God. The dictionary records it that the reader may mark that the shepherd seeks the sheep until he find it, and bears it home upon his own shoulders, rejoicing.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that salvation begins not in the sinner’s search for God but in God’s search for the sinner. The sheep does not find the shepherd; the Good Shepherd seeks the lost, and seeks until He find it, and loseth none that the Father hath given Him. This is the effectual seeking grace of Christ, who is come to seek and to save that which was lost, and who giveth His life for the sheep. So the Scripture teaches the helplessness of the lost and the sovereignty of the seeking love that finds them; and it tells of the joy in heaven over one sinner that repenteth.
roots_summary: From the Greek probaton, sheep, the parable names the shepherd who seeks the one lost sheep until he find it.

usage: Like the shepherd seeking the lost sheep, God seeks the sinner before ever the sinner seeks Him.

etymology: From the Greek drachmē, a silver coin of a day’s wage; the parable of the woman who sweeps the house to find one piece of silver.
biblical_def: The parable of the Lost Coin is the companion of the Lost Sheep, and like it sets forth the diligent seeking of the lost and the joy that follows their recovery. Either what woman, said the LORD, having ten pieces of silver, if she lose one piece, doth not light a candle, and sweep the house, and seek diligently till she find it? And when she hath found it, she calleth her friends and her neighbours together, saying, Rejoice with me; for I have found the piece which I had lost (Luk 15:8-9). And He gave the meaning: Likewise, I say unto you, there is joy in the presence of the angels of God over one sinner that repenteth (Luk 15:10). The dictionary marks this parable beside its fellow, the two teaching one truth under two figures. The sheep wanders abroad and is sought in the wilderness; the coin lies lost within the house, dark and unmindful of its own loss, and is sought by candle and broom till it be found. So the Scripture shows the sinner lost not only in open wandering but in dead and senseless insensibility, unable even to know himself lost; and it shows the diligence of the seeking grace that lights the candle, sweeps the house, and searches till the lost be found. The coin bears the image of its owner, marred and hidden in the dust, even as fallen man bears the defaced image of his Maker; and the joy of the finding is the joy of heaven, in the presence of the angels of God, over one sinner that repenteth.
webster_summary: The parable in which a woman sweeps the house to find one lost coin, and rejoices with her neighbours when it is found.

She lighteth a candle and sweepeth the house and seeketh diligently till she find it.
When she hath found it, she calleth her friends to rejoice with her.
There is joy in the presence of the angels of God over one sinner that repenteth.
The coin pictures the sinner lost in senseless insensibility, sought by grace.

corruption_paragraphs: The parable of the Lost Coin has drawn little redefinition from the present age, surviving as the companion of the Lost Sheep in the LORD’s threefold answer to the murmuring of the Pharisees. The dictionary records it that the reader may mark the candle lighted and the house swept till the lost coin be found.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the sinner is lost not only in open wandering but in dead and senseless insensibility, unable even to know himself lost, like a coin fallen in the dust. The seeking grace of God lights the candle, sweeps the house, and searches diligently till the lost be found; for the coin cannot seek itself. The defaced image upon the silver pictures the marred image of God in fallen man, recovered by Him who seeks it; and the joy of the finding is the joy of heaven, in the presence of the angels of God, over one sinner that repenteth.

etymology: From the Latin prodigus, “wasteful,” through the son who wasted his substance; the parable of the lost son and the father’s free grace.
biblical_def: The parable of the Prodigal Son is the third and greatest of the LORD’s parables of the lost, crowning the Lost Sheep and the Lost Coin with the fullest picture of repentance and free grace. A certain man had two sons; and the younger took his portion, and gathered all together, and took his journey into a far country, and there wasted his substance with riotous living (Luk 15:13). When a famine arose and he was brought to feed swine and to hunger for their husks, he came to himself, and said, I will arise and go to my father, and will say unto him, Father, I have sinned against heaven, and before thee, and am no more worthy to be called thy son (Luk 15:18-19). And while he was yet a great way off, his father saw him, and had compassion, and ran, and fell on his neck, and kissed him (Luk 15:20); and he clothed him in the best robe, and put a ring on his hand, and killed the fatted calf, for this my son was dead, and is alive again; he was lost, and is found (Luk 15:24). The dictionary marks this parable as the great word on repentance and the Father’s free grace. The son’s coming to himself, his arising, his confession of sin, are the marks of a true repentance wrought in the heart; and the father’s running, embracing, and feasting are the free and overflowing grace that receives the penitent. Yet the elder brother, angry and self-righteous, will not go in (Luk 15:28), and is also rebuked; so the parable warns both the prodigal and the proud.
webster_summary: The parable in which a wasteful son returns confessing his sin, and the father runs to receive him with free and joyful grace.
webster_full: THE PRODIGAL SON, the parable of the lost son and the father’s free grace.
The younger son wasteth his substance with riotous living in a far country.
Brought to want, he cometh to himself and ariseth to confess his sin.
While he is yet a great way off, the father runneth and receiveth him with joy.
The elder brother, angry and self-righteous, is also rebuked.
scriptures: And not many days after the younger son gathered all together, and took his journey into a far country, and there wasted his substance with riotous living.
I will arise and go to my father, and will say unto him, Father, I have sinned against heaven, and before thee,
And he arose, and came to his father. But when he was yet a great way off, his father saw him, and had compassion, and ran, and fell on his neck, and kissed him.
For this my son was dead, and is alive again; he was lost, and is found. And they began to be merry.
corruption_summary: A parable misread by the modern age as the universal fatherhood of God and a welcome that needs no atonement or repentance; the Scripture itself rebuts the error.
corruption_paragraphs: The parable of the Prodigal Son is, of all the parables, the one most pressed into the service of a modern corruption. It is preached as the proof of the universal fatherhood of God — that every man is already a son, and the gospel is only the announcement of an unconditional welcome that needs neither atonement nor repentance. In this reading the father’s running embrace becomes a divine affirmation of the sinner as he is, and the cross is made needless; some go so far as to call it the heart of a universalist hope, that the Father will at last receive all without exception, sin or no sin, return or no return.

The Scripture itself rebuts the error. The son was no son in fellowship while he wasted his substance; he was dead, and lost (Luk 15:24), and his restoration came not while he sat among the swine but when he came to himself, and arose, and confessed, Father, I have sinned against heaven, and before thee (Luk 15:18). The feast rests upon grace, but it is grace that receives a penitent, not grace that excuses impenitence; the welcome is free, yet it is the welcome of one returning in repentance. And the elder brother’s cold self-righteousness, which would earn the father’s goods by service, is rebuked no less than the younger’s riot; so the parable strikes down both the licence that presumes upon grace and the pride that despises it. It says nothing of a fatherhood common to all men apart from Christ; it tells how a lost son is brought home by repentance to a Father whose grace is free.
roots_summary: From the Latin prodigus, “wasteful,” the Prodigal Son names the lost son restored by repentance to the father’s free grace.
